articles.text: Piedmont City Council received an informational update on Reach code implementation from city Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman and Climate Action fellow Annie Wensley at a meeting on Tuesday, May 2. Reach codes (Ordinance 750 N.S.) went into effect on June 1, 2021. The amendment was adopted by Piedmont’s City Council on February 1, 2021 and affects the sales and transfers of real estate and the construction of new and existing residential buildings. Reach codes require certain home renovation projects to include energy efficiency measures or photovoltaic systems. Additionally, Ordinance 751 N.S., or the home energy assessment policy, went into effect on March 3, 2021 and affects homeowners and real estate agents. When selling a property or transferring the title, the seller must provide potential buyers with a Home Energy Score or Home Energy Audit prepared in the past five years, in addition to the normal disclosure information. In preparation for the adoption of a 2022 Energy Code, city staff have conducted ongoing evaluations of the reach codes enacted in 2021, heralded by the city’s Sustainability Department. articles.text: Piedmont resident Eric Havian gave a presentation at the April 27 school board meeting on preventing gun violence. Havian, who has been involved with Brady United, the national gun control organization, for nearly 40 years, proposed to the board steps that can be taken to raise awareness of parents and students. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, commonly known as the Brady Bill, was passed by Congress in 1993 after James Brady, the White House Press Secretary was permanently disabled from a gunshot wound during the attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan in 1991. The law requires federal background checks for all gun purchases and a five-day waiting period on purchases. Havian made proposals of actions the school district can take which focus on the safety of children by communicating with parents the importance of gun safety. “I’m guilty of this myself. Many times [we] think Piedmont is immune to a lot of the problems of violence, that are in the other communities in the Bay Area. But we are not,” said Havian. Havian’s advice would give the school district a leading opportunity to implement what may soon be a state requirement. articles.text: Barber Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and their seven-year-old son, Vlad, recently set out on an unimaginable journey. On April 1, they gathered a few personal belongings, stuffed them into a couple of suitcases and left their war-torn home in the Donbass region of Ukraine to make a new life in America. “The military operations (in Ukraine) were drawing out all the resources.” Alex said. “As long as the country is at war, it cannot be prosperous and does not offer a good future. It is simply too dangerous to live there.” The family drove from Crimea to Moscow, then to Lithuania and on to Warsaw, Poland before flying to Paris, Madrid and Mexico City. They arrived in Tijuana on April 11 at the same time the Piedmont Community Church Mexico house-building mission was taking place. Church member Scott Willis was onsite in Tijuana helping Piedmont students and adult leaders tackle the task of building 12 homes for families in need. Willis is also the chair of the church’s Refugee Task Force, a group that has helped settle families from Afghanistan, Pakistan and Syria. Willis made contact with the family through a former Mexico mission participant, Jenny Miller-Feinberg, who works for Bayer, Inc. Alex’s brother, who also works for Bayer, had posted on the company’s intranet bulletin board the need for housing for his brother and family who were already on their way to the U.S. Piedmont Community Church members Bob and Judy Wright obtained plane tickets for the family to fly to Oakland, and Kirk and Christina Miller, Jenny’s parents, met them at the airport on April 13 and offered to host the family on an ongoing basis. “Of course, we calmed down when we got to Piedmont,” Alex said. “We are finally in a safe place where we can feel comfortable, but at the same time, we are worried about our parents and loved ones who stayed in our city. We have feelings of anxiety.” While they are now physically secure, Maryna finds the current situation emotionally difficult. “I have relatives still in Photo by Michael Barber Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and their seven-year-old son, Vlad pose for a family photo taken in the courtyard of Piedmont Community Church after attending services on April 24. Ukraine who I miss,” Maryna said. “I understand that there is no future in my country, but my heart is there, and I ache for those places, and for the people left there.” Vlad, the couple’s son, has already begun attending Wildwood School and is adapting nicely. “I thought that it would be much more difficult for Vlad to be in this school since he does not understand English,” Maryna said. “Surprisingly, he feels good and goes to school in a good mood. He likes his new teacher, who he says is kinder than the teacher he had in Ukraine.” In addition to sharpening their English-speaking skills and learning the rules of the Bay Area roads, Alex and Maryna are seeking employment. They will require the services of an immigration attorney to file the necessary paperwork to obtain jobs. Alex was trained as a mechanical engineer and worked in agriculture, while Maryna worked in accounting. Piedmont Church is asking for donations through their website, PiedmontChurch.org, to help with legal fees and transitioning. “We are infinitely grateful to people and the church that helps us at the moment,” Alex said. Last week, Vlad told his parents that the children in his new class treat him well. “He brought home a postcard from a classmate who expressed his feelings,” Maryna said. “He wants to be friends with him.” To donate to the Piedmont Community Church Refugee Task Force, visit PiedmontChurch.org and click ‘Giving.’ hours.

articles.text: The Diversity Film series continues with a screening of Power to Heal tomorrow, Thursday, May 5. The screening is being co-hosted by the City of Piedmont, Adult Education Program, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee (PADC). A Zoom webinar will feature The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long documentary movie describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. articles.text: The Piedmont Advanced Learners Program Support (ALPS) parent group held a forum last Thursday night, April 28, in the high school library to better define what “Academic Excellence” means to Piedmont residents. More than 40 parents were in attendance for the event led by ALPS President Michael Malione and Vice President Ella Grossberg. ALPS is a longstanding group of parents with the goal of pursuing high academic standards and providing resources to accelerate opportunities and joy in learning. In the two-hour meeting, parents broke into groups for English Language Arts (ELA), Math, and Science for a chance for everyone to speak and be heard. Participants identified gaps they’ve encountered between expectations and recent experiences with the strength of academics in the school district. Concerns included both the elementary and middle school foundations in reading and mathematics, as well as more specific programs and courses at the high school level. Parents espoused the virtues of a path for rigorous education that solidifies foundational skills and growing subject depth over time. This reporter joined the English and Language Arts group, at which Beach parent Esti Iturralde explained the benefits of building a knowledge base and excitement on topics through reading before focusing on analysis. Many attendees said they believe the school district should look beyond the California State educational standards, which address statewide declines in student proficiency not being seen in Piedmont. Attendees included two high school teachers, Science Chair Andy Willats and Math Department Head Kate Waldron, and a school district administrator. Some parents of high school students requested that the school district have a curriculum consistent with and in support of how the College Board defines its AP curricula. Parents also expressed the need for Piedmont High School to offer more AP courses like AP Physics. The argument for a return to more of a quantitative focus in the high school science curriculum was commonly voiced. A general sentiment expressed from the participants was that the academic strength of Piedmont’s education has been declining for a number of years. According to US News and World Education in 2022, Piedmont High ranked #237 nationally and #30 in California. In 2008, Piedmont was ranked #64 nationally. Rankings come from performance on state-required tests, graduation rates and preparation for college. For details go to: Usnews.com/education/besthigh-schools/california/districts/ piedmont-city-unified-school-district/piedmont-high-school-3029 Parents recognized that funding is a part of the equation but felt that the school district needs to focus more strongly on the strengths and needs of its students who are having a more difficult time getting into the universities of their first choice. The April 28 meeting was the first of several forums hosted by ALPS, which has been Piedmont’s leading advocate for curricular excellence and the provider of resources and events that foster academic attainment for more than a decade. For more information visit PiedmontALPS.org . articles.text: Much attention has been focused on the importance of early foreign language learning. Some research reports that younger children learn languages better than older children and adults. With so many demands already placed on children, parents ask if it is important that a child learn a second language at a young age. What program options are available? Benefits of knowing a second language In addition to developing a lifelong ability to communicate with people from other countries and backgrounds, other benefits include improved overall school performance and superior problem-solving skills. Students of foreign languages tend to score higher on standardized tests. Results from the SAT show that students who studied a foreign language for 4 or more years outscored other students on the verbal and math portions of the test. Knowledge of a second language also seems to coincide with high academic achievement. One study shows that students who were in “rigorous” programs in high school, which included 3 years of foreign language study, were likely to earn better grades in college. Learning another language can enhance knowledge of English structure and vocabulary. The benefits to society are many. Americans fluent in other languages improve global communication, enhance our economic competitiveness abroad, and maintain political and security interests. In recent years, the U.S. government has expressed a need for fluent speakers of languages other than English, particularly in less commonly taught languages such as Arabic and Chinese. Learning a language at any age is beneficial. Some studies have shown that the human brain is more open to linguistic development during the years between birth and pre-adolescence and that children who learn a language before the onset of adolescence are more likely to develop native-like pronunciation. When children have an early start to a long sequence of language instruction that continues through high school and college, they will be able to achieve levels of fluency that have not been possible in the past due to the late start of most language programs. At the same time, older children and adults can still be successful at learning a second language, although the level of attainment may be less predictable because of factors that can influence language learning. Any exposure to a second language and culture is beneficial, even if native-like proficiency is not the goal or the outcome. Options available in Piedmont The types of language programs available can be placed on a continuum. At one end of the continuum are immersion programs, which offer the greatest amount of time in language study and produce students with the highest levels of proficiency. Participants identified gaps they’ve encountered between expectations and recent experiences with the strength of academics in the school district. Parents espoused the virtues of a path for rigorous education that solidifies foundational skills and growing subject depth over time. This reporter joined the English and Language Arts group, at which Beach parent Esti Iturralde explained the benefits of building a knowledge base and excitement on topics through reading before focusing on analysis. Many attendees said they believe the school district should look beyond the California State educational standards, which address statewide declines in student proficiency not being seen in Piedmont. Attendees included two high school teachers, Science Chair Andy Willats and Math Department Head Kate Waldron, and a school district administrator. Some parents of high school students requested that the school district have a curriculum consistent with and in support of how the College Board defines its AP curricula. Parents also expressed the need for Piedmont High School to offer more AP courses like AP Physics. The argument for a return to more of a quantitative focus in the high school science curriculum was commonly voiced. A general sentiment expressed from the participants was that the academic strength of Piedmont’s education has been declining for a number of years. Many families are thinking about Why and when should my child learn a second language? Much attention has been focused on the importance of early foreign language learning. Some research reports that younger children learn languages better than older children and adults. With so many demands already placed on children, parents ask if it is important that a child learn a second language at a young age. What program options are available? Benefits of knowing a second language In addition to developing a lifelong ability to communicate with people from other countries and backgrounds, other benefits include improved overall school performance and superior problem-solving skills. Students of foreign languages tend to score higher on standardized tests. Results from the SAT show that students who studied a foreign language for 4 or more years outscored other students on the verbal and math portions of the test. Knowledge of a second language also seems to coincide with high academic achievement. One study shows that students who were in “rigorous” programs in high school, which included 3 years of foreign language study, were likely to earn better grades in college. Learning another language can enhance knowledge of English structure and vocabulary. The benefits to society are many. Americans fluent in other languages improve global communication, enhance our economic competitiveness abroad, and maintain political and security interests. In recent years, the U.S. government has expressed a need for fluent speakers of languages other than English, particularly in less commonly taught languages such as Arabic and Chinese. articles.text: Readmont, a community-wide reading project in its 12th year, will culminate with an evening of guest speakers on May 19 and will be on Zoom. Hosted by Piedmont High School librarian Kathryn Levenson and English department chair Beth Black, the event will include a discussion of this year’s selection, A Thousand Splendid Suns, a novel by Afghani-American author Khaled Hosseini. A panel discussion will follow with a discussion of women’s rights and refugees by Fouzia Azizi, Director of Refugee Services for Jewish Family and Community Services of the East Bay, and Humaira Khan of Toronto, Canada, an expert on women’s rights in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The event will be held on Zoom on Thursday, May 19, from 7:00 to 8:00 p.m. A Thousand Splendid Suns chronicles the story of two women living in Kabul, Afghanistan. The book is appropriate for ages 14 and up. For younger readers, the English Department recommends the book I am Malala for ages 10 to 14, and Malala, My Story of Standing up for Girls’ Rights, appropriate for age 6 through 10. “We chose this book for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay area,” said Black. Books may be checked out from the library at any Piedmont school. Books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, and are available for purchase with a 20% discount at A Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair, 6120 La Salle Avenue. Questions may be addressed to Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or to Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Jabbar Weaver On April 23, researchers from the University of Delaware shared the results of a landmark study of Reading Recovery, a common literacy intervention for young children. Reading Recovery popularized an alternative to phonics—an approach called MSV, which teaches children to decipher words using a complex analysis of multiple cues (MSV stands for “meaning, syntax, and visual”). Kids learn to infer the word from “what makes sense,” “what sounds right,” and using clues from the story illustrations, in addition to considering the letters in the word. The study—funded by the US Department of Education, including more than 9,000 students, and led by authors who had studied Reading Recovery for more than a decade—found surprising results. Students who received Reading Recovery in 1st grade made shortterm progress, but they lost all their gains and actually did worse by 3rd and 4th grade compared to a control group. What went wrong? One explanation for the disappointing results is that MSV (also known as “three-cueing”) has been discredited by other research, including findings from the 2000 National Reading Panel and subsequent studies. MSV is commonly used in Piedmont schools and is thought to be especially problematic for students with learning differences and those from less advantaged backgrounds. Decades of evidence highlight the critical role of phonics and that MSV distracts kids away from learning phonics. This latest study sheds new light on a decades-old controversy that has recently been reignited. Literacy experts such as Professor Lucy Calkins—the author of Piedmont’s main literacy curriculum—have now revised their materials to discourage using MSV with students. “We have changed important things…. We emphasize to teachers that when a child is stuck on a tricky word, the best response is ‘look at the letters,’” wrote Dr. Calkins in an April 1 blog post to teachers. What does this mean for Piedmont? Piedmont schools, stressed by the demands of the pandemic, have made gradual shifts away from instruction grounded in MSV. PUSD leaders will present an update on literacy curriculum at the upcoming May 11 school board meeting. However, removing MSV from teaching is no easy task. MSV is embedded throughout Piedmont’s early reading instruction—from the classroom books, to our benchmark assessment, to our curriculum for struggling readers: Leveled Literacy Intervention, which is based on Reading Recovery. These long-term findings on a MSV-focused program may stir doubts for Piedmont parents whose kids appeared to benefit from Leveled Literacy Intervention in 1st grade only to see continued struggles in later grades. Many families have hired private tutors to get the strong foundational skills instruction their kids need to catch up. But, what happens to students whose families do not have the necessary knowledge or resources to get that help? It’s critical for teachers and families to have up-to-date information on evidence-based practices. A group of Piedmont parents and educators have formed a support group to share ideas on helping all kids become strong readers. Want to learn more? Drop us a line at piedmontreading@gmail.com Esti Iturralde, PhD is a licensed clinical psychologist and Piedmont parent. Jabbar Weaver is a 25-year teacher and principal, a member of the California and Oakland NAACP Education Committees, and Co-Founder of FULCRUM (Full and Complete Reading is a Universal Mandate)

articles.text: Piedmont High School science teacher John Savage invited the Post into his Period 5 Chemistry class on Friday, April 8 to observe a titration lab in action. The class of sophomores was tasked with finding the concentration of an unknown hydrochloric acid solution while discovering the functions of science instruments none of them had used prior. PHS purchased new lab equipment via grant money from the Makers Club and the Piedmont Parents Club. In the lab, a solution of acid and water sat in a beaker with a solution above it that slowly dropped a base into the acid. For the first time students used a digital pH probe which was connected to a laptop graphing the change in pH as the base dropped. “We haven’t used the pH recorder or the drop recorder, so this lab was interesting to learn how to use them,” said 10th grader Jonah Dupree. “The purpose of the lab was to measure what the concentration of the Hydrochloric acid is, so we are going to do that by finding data like the level of the pH of the solution in order to find the concentration.” The drop recorder had to be calibrated prior to use, and it digitally took record of how many drops of the basic solution were needed to turn the acid solution to a neutral 7 pH. The calibration process gave students a measurement equating the number of drops per mL. Students learned first-hand how to solve an equation with Thomas Worthington (left), Mateo DeVries, and Will Becker watch closely as Alex Aires measures a volume of base for their titration lab. Macy Puckett (left) and Isabella Wire check the pH graph on their computer while Ali Gallacher makes sure the drop counter is aligned properly. John Savage demostrates the lab for his class. two knowns, the volume of the acid and the concentration of the base, along with the discovered volume of the base to determine the concentration of the acid. Labs like this were missing from Piedmont during distance learning. “Being back in a laboratory for a science class has different challenges compared with doing it online through distance learning. In-person class is definitely challenging in some aspects, but there is a lot of knowledge to learn,” said sophomore Ray Gentemann. Savage divided students up into table groups, emphasized the importance of using goggles while using acids and let them loose to experiment. Savage, a PHS graduate of 2005 himself, frequently gathered the class around exemplary set ups to demonstrate the processes and instruments new to the whole class. “The instructions on the paper were kind of confusing but once [Mr. Savage] explained it, it really made sense,” said Siddharth Bhatia, whose group’s setup was shown to the class as an example by Savage on a number of occasions. Towards the end of the period Savage drew the class’ attention to another new tool, a volumentric flask that only measures to 1000 mL. “This container is good for one thing and one thing only, measuring exactly to 1000 mL. Why would that be? What use does this have?” he asked. The neck of this bulbous container is skinny, giving a measurement with a high level of accuracy and small room for differentiation as liquid fills up to the only line of measurement. Abstract concepts and foreign instruments are used in Savage’s class, a class that requires a challenging level of plasticity of the mind to question, contemplate and discover. In less than two hours the class acquired a new skill, titration, and received their first experience with several new instruments. Savage’s classes have long been favored by students and his commitment to achieving the honorable, the high school motto, were on display that afternoon. Spencer Barlow (left) and Jonah Dupree work as a pair setting up their experiment. John Savage shows his class what their graphs mapping pH levels should look like when the pH probe is connected to their laptops. Ali Gallacher measures the appropriate amount of base for her group using a pipette.

Playing at Chabot College on Friday and Saturday, April 29-30, Piedmont’s tennis team came home with some impressive achievements. German foreign exchange student Lenni Burchardt, a junior, advanced to the singles finals and settled for 2nd place in the tournament. Ben Breber and Monte Imburg teamed up to placed third in the doubles ladder. Burchardt entered as the No. 4 seed and defeated No. 1 Elijah Cho from Berkeley in the semifinals in straight sets, 6-3, 6-3, using his powerful forehand and backhand for winning points. “It was a good game. Everything was working pretty well, My serve was landing and my form was better than usual. It feels good to hit winners because I’m not a very patient player,” said Burchardt with a laugh. Prior to Saturday’s semis and finals, Burchardt defeated Castro Valley’s Josh Kuwana in the first round, 6-0, 6-0, and Berkeley’s Michael Alaharazy in the second round, 6-2, 6-2. Burchardt lost to Berkeley’s Leighton Sproul in the finals, 6-1, 6-2. Sproul did well to return hard forehands by quickly lobbing shots back over the net. articles.text: The much-awaited next step for the Piedmont’s varsity football program finally occurred. After more than a month of searching, the high school has announced the hiring of Jordan Seiden, a former head coach at Skyline High in Oakland. He was hired on April 26 and will start planning for Spring Ball this week. Seiden grew up in Berkeley and played at St. Mary’s High School before playing collegiately for UC Davis as a receiver and running back from 1992- 1995. He was a classmate of Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame 2014 inductee Rich Watts while at Davis. He comes with pedigree of coaching, working under local legend and former San Jose State head coach Alonzo Carter as McClymond’s offensive coordinator in 2005-2006. He also worked under former 25-year Bishop O’Dowd head coach Paul Perenon in the early 2000s. “I’m born and raised in Berkeley and played for St. Mary’s. It’s funny, one of the only pictures I have left from those days are of a run I had against Piedmont. I played two years at Diablo Valley College and transferred to UC Davis. I returned to Berkeley where I got my first chance to coach, and then I had the opportunity to coach under Paul Perenon while he was at Bishop O’Dowd. It was a terrific opportunity,” said Seiden. “Alonzo and Paul were all about focus and hard work. All the things that attracted me to football were [being able to work] with coaches like that. They held themselves to high expectations,” he added. Seiden was most recently the head coach at Skyline High in 2018. Prior to Skyline, He took several years off of coaching to watch his son, Jordan Jr., play football for Moreau Catholic. Seiden was the offensive coordinator at Arroyo from 2011-2012, was Cupuchino’s head coach in 2010, offensive coordinator at Contra Costa College in 2009, and head coach at Castro Valley in 2007-2008. Earlier he was McClymonds’ offensive coordinator (2005- 2006), Berkeley’s defensive coordinator (2004), Chabot College’s defensive backs coach (2003), a Berkeley offensive assistant (2002), Bishop O’Dowd’s JV head coach (2000-2001), Berkeley’s DBs coach (1999), O’Dowd assisPiedmont High finalized its long search for a head football coach by hiring Jordan Seiden. tant (1998), Diablo Valley College’s linebackers coach (1997), and Berkeley’s DBs coach to start his coaching career in 1996. He currently works in the Oakland School District as a case manager, giving him a wealth of experience with students from a wide range of backgrounds. “It really helps with communication and understanding. I have a firm line with kids, but I know how to bring myself to their level. It helps bridge the gap. Kids are kids and they all need guidance and support in their own special way,” he said. Seiden walks into a situation where he’s tasked with building a new a culture of football in Piedmont, a school that has had football teams for more than 100 years. The team has had fewer kids signing up since Covid changed lives more than two years ago. “Building a culture comes with how you present yourself. There’s always positive energy with new coaches. If you can maintain that you can develop a culture. When I was growing up, Piedmont was a very good program and put out a lot of good players over the years. I played against Richie Watts (Piedmont’s quarterback in 1988-89( and got to know him at Davis. It starts with the foundation and how you build. If you have the right people to help build one step at a time, you have a really good opportunity.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco launched an exhibition entitled Still Lives in Contemporary Art on March 31. The exhibition will be on view through August 12. The group exhibition brings together an international group of artists who have unique takes on contemporary art and still life. The artists have created works within a framework of Black diasporic identities, histories, and collective experiences. Featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Brittney Leeanne Williams, Untitled (Birds of Paradise), 2018. Acrylic on canvas. 10 x 10 in. Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. The exhibit is on the third floor gallery. To make a reservation, visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibitions/elegies-still-lifesin-contemporary-art.

articles.text: A scene from The Farewell, written and directed by Lulu Wang. The Farewell is in so many ways remarkable, a nuanced and yet explicit film about what it means to leave your country of origin and come to America and be confronted by a spectrum of language, norms, attitudes and behavior that can seem overwhelming and all but insurmountable. At the outset, the process of acculturation can be an exhausting and demanding journey. Once made, it is never completely over. The Farewell focuses on one closely held norm that seems uniquely Chinese and comes into conflict with the values of a thoroughly Americanized young woman. Written and directed by Lulu Wang, she captures with insight and humor as well high stakes seriousness just how complex and multilayered culture can be. And how painful it is to live rooted in two places at the same time. For the central character Billi (Awkwafina), a twenty-something New Yorker, those two places are America and China. She came to the U.S. at the age of six with her mom, Jian (Diana Lin), and her father Haiyan (Tzi Ma). In the opening scenes Billi is told by her parents that her much loved grandmother, Nai Nai (Shuzhen Zhov), diagnosed with stagefour lung cancer, has only a few months to live. Billi learns that her family has made two decisions immediately: first, by agreement of family members in New York and China, they will not to tell Nai Nai the truth regarding her illness. Secondly, the family will leave for city of Changchun in China within the week, using the imminent wedding of a nephew as an excuse to gather, but in effect to say goodbye to Nai Nai. Billi, however, is told that she must remain behind. The reason being that the family does not trust her to keep the secret from her grandmother; she’s too emotional, her connection to Nai Nai such that she will break down when the two meet. Billi, of course, has also made clear that she feels her grandmother should be told the truth. And this is only act one. Unbeknownst to her parents, Billi takes a later flight and arrives at her grandmother’s home just as the now extended family is getting ready to sit down to the first of many meals. They all watch Billi closely, anticipating that she will reveal to Nai Nai the truth. articles.text: A scene from Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home. The first Free Willy movie made such a splash, so to speak, that it was inevitable there would be a sequel. After all, what’s not to like? An orphaned, malcontent street kid named Jesse, age 12 (played by Jason James Richter), on the verge of becoming a teenager, is rescued by a 7,000-pound orca, and the tween manages to do the same for Willy. Literally. The enduring strength of the franchise is that Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home also has at its center a family theme. The most immediate difference is that Jesse is now a newbie 14-year-old teen, and has settled nicely in with his foster parents, Glen and Annie Greenwoods (Michael Madsen and Jane Atkinson). Sadly, Jesse discovers that his long ago missing mother has passed away; however, to his surprise he discovers that he has a younger half-brother called Elvis (Frank Capra), who comes to visit and is generously taken in by the Greenwoods. He’s a fast-talking wiseacre who would rather tell a fib, even if the truth would serve just as well. To make things even more interesting, and given that there are teen hormones all in a swirl, Jesse is introduced to Nadine (Kate Schellhardt), his age, who is the granddaughter of the theme park’s handyman, Randolph (August Schellenberg), a Native American. They have immediate chemistry, hence there will be, of course, an innocent kiss in their future. And so the adventure begins. The Greenwoods suggest that the family take a brief holiday to the ocean. Jesse is sitting in a cove, playing his harmonica, looking out at the Pacific, when, to his amazement, Willy appears. Only this time, the now massive orca is in the company of his pod family. It’s a joyous reunion for both, and Jesse rides Willy in the surf and Nadine joins them as well. To add to the developing narrative, the kids discover that there is a grounded tanker not far off shore, which is leaking oil into the ocean, a spill that threatens all the sea life in the area, most especially Willy and his pod. If the oil gets into the orcas blowholes it could prove fatal. The question now posed is: what can the kids do to prevent what will be an ecological disaster? Adding to the tension is the plan by the owners of the tanker and the greedy owners of the theme park to capture Willy and return him to the theme park in order to perform once again. There are countless narrow escapes. A marine biologist, Kate Haley (Elizabeth Pena), shows up and explains that if the whales are not able to escape the oil spill (they are now trapped in the cove) it will prove deadly to the pod. Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home will once again engage a younger audience as they root for Jesse, Nadine and Elvis Elvis, and in their common cause to save the whales. As sequels go, it’s a winner. articles.text: Recently I spotted an article in the New York Times by columnist Ross Douthat regarding the demise (he uses the word “end”) of movies as we, for generations, have come to known them. My answer would be yes, and no. However I would add to his analysis the impact the global pandemic has had on what was once a cultural phenomenon – walking into a darkened room and watching with strangers a larger than life story told on an expansive screen, one still framed, on occasion, by heavy felt curtains. My response to the word “end” is that Hollywood will, of course, continue to make movies predicated on the conviction that we love to be told a story. We can easily imagine our antecedents sitting around campfires, listening to dramatic tales told and retold, recounting the countless variations of the then human experience, each filled with embellished magic. I would suggest that this is not the end of the narrative feature; rather, it is the beginning of what I think of as our post-pandemic movie-viewing period. What has changed is the way that feature films are today created and delivered. Well before the pandemic, movies were being watched on screens of all sizes, from large, wall-mounted televisions, to computers, to hand held smart phones, The stories were enhanced when needed by CGI (computer-generated imagery). But what brought this technology truly mainstream was the government Covid019 quarantine mandate. Seemingly overnight, theaters became hothouses of the virus. The very air in enclosed spaces was and continues to be a possible threat as were the people in the seats before and behind. The alternative to going to the theater quickly became obvious: view movies in the safety of your home. And so the word “streaming” became part of the lexicon, a panoply of choices delivered by a host of subscription-driven companies, examples being Netflix, Prime, Hulu, VUDU/, HBO, and Showtime. In trying to avoid slipping into hyperbole, this change has been revolutionary and culture changing, equated with the now ubiquitous cellphone (which I generously compare to Gutenberg’s invention of type-setting print). My prediction is that even when Covid and variants are regarded with just another form of the flu (with annual vaccinations offered), we will not return to the theater, and even the term blockbuster will take on a much-diminished definition. As Douthat points out in his piece, even this year’s 10 films nominated for Academy Awards, which shared a bevy of top-tier actors, major directors, as well as classic genres such as epics or meet-cute romances, well, almost nobody went to see them (nine out of the ten made less than $40 million in box office revenue). As a result more and more recent releases are now opening simultaneously in theaters and streaming for home viewing. The question begged is: Even when this awful virus is behind us, will the movie-going audience ever return in the pre-pandemic numbers experienced in 2019 and before? Douthat, for one, suggests that 1990 was the peak. And will the annual Oscars ceremony ever again be compelling, or find am audience or generate the anticipation it once found in those halcyon days of the 20th century when movie stars were iconic celebrities, larger than life? Have they too been diminished down to what Douthat opines as ordinary size and now regarded as simply part of the viewed content? We’ll soon find out.

articles.text: Spring green is the theme for this quick salad that announces much-awaited spring vegetables. After so many months of kale, collards and broccoli, sugar snap peas at farmers markets signal a big shift in what we’ll have on our plates for the coming weeks. Sugar snap peas are a variety where the tender pod is eaten along with the pea inside. They are adorably plump and tender, a rightful star of this quick salad. pages.text: Wednesday, May 4, 2022 23 INGREDIENTS Snappy Pea and Spinach Salad ideal for early summer By Deborah Quok Spring green is the theme for this quick salad that announces much-awaited spring vegetables. After so many months of kale, collards and broccoli, sugar snap peas at farmers markets signal a big shift in what we’ll have on our plates for the coming weeks. Sugar snap peas are a variety where the tender pod is eaten along with the pea inside. They are adorably plump and tender, a rightful star of this quick salad. (An Asian-style snow pea is similar but has a flat pod.) Just remember to remove the string that runs along the length of the pod. I make a version of this salad when sugar snap peas are prolific (read: a bit more affordable) at my favorite farmers’ stands. It’s an easy adjustment to use asparagus, sliced cucumbers, and/or radishes, if you enjoy those options, but sometimes a few exquisite ingredients are all that are needed for a perfectly satisfying salad. I leave everything raw as I love the taste of fresh, raw sweet peas. And the crunch. But feel free to do a quick blanch in boiling water, then a plunge into an ice water bath, if that’s how you prefer. Admittedly this does result in a showier, bright green snap pea. Hopefully this will be a springboard into multiple variations to enjoy in the coming months. For the dressing: • 2 tablespoons lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 2 tablespoons fresh mint, minced • 1/2 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, to taste For the salad: • 10 ounces sugar snap peas, sliced thinly on a steep diagonal • 6 ounces baby spinach, the size of a typical bag of triple-washed greens • 1/4 cup chives, cut in 1/2-inch lengths INSTRUCITONS Sugar Snap Pea and Spinach Salad with Lemony Mint Dressing. For the dressing: Combine the mustard, lemon juice, sea salt and pepper in a small bowl and mix well. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil, whisking to help emulsify the dressing. Add the minced mint. Set aside while you prepare the salad. For the salad: 1. Rinse the sugar snap peas and remove the tough string that runs down the length of the pod where the peas are attached inside. Slice on a steep diagonal, maybe 4 – 5 slices depending on the size of the pod. 2. Slice the chives in 1/ 2-inch lengths 3. Add the sliced sugar snap peas to a 3-quart bowl. Add the dressing and gently toss. Add the chives and spinach and toss again to distribute the dressing throughout. This is a very lightly dressed salad, which we prefer, so the delicate flavor of the sugar snap peas shines through. articles.text: An excellent turnout of 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend was on hand for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays outing April 27, a beautiful morning in Piedmont. It was announced that former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a tour of Tyson Lake, in two weeks, on Sunday, May 15. Last week, April 27 the walkers enjoyed the second of two walking tours of Piedmont front gardens that were part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” Hope Salzer, a Board member of Piedmont Connect, led the walkers to the first garden the previous week, Hope’s own garden on Cambrian Avenue. This week took the group to the second garden belong to Nancy McKee-Jolda and Rob Jolda on Harvard Road. To qualify for the Natives Garden Tour, gardens were requited to have at least 70% California native plants. The walkers went down Highland to Wildwood Avenue, and then Prospect Road which ends at Harvard Road. Nancy told the group that she had been inspired some years earlier during a trip to France. The “Monet gardens” made her want to create her own lovely garden. Hiking in the East Bay Regional Parks also provided a fascination about what our area looked like 150 years ago, and it motivate Nancy to “jump into nature and native gardens.” She found that she loved gardening and the lifecycle process of plants going from seed to flower and back to seed again. All the seasons provide a rich garden experience for her. Nancy shared a list of 24 succulents, shrubs & large bushes, and flowering plants in her garden, and identified many of them for the group. They included Douglas irises, different buckwheat varieties, mugworts, purple Self-Heals, huckleberry, wild roses, and a mock orange with its first buds. She noted that many of these native plants were used by indigenous people as medicines and for teas. Explaining her native plants garden, Nancy said, “My intent was to show how ‘natural’ such a garden is, how simple and attractive and important.” Nancy’s husband, Rob, said how much he appreciates the work she has done with the garden. As the group was preparing to leave, Noemi Alvarado had a visitor, daughter-in-law Libby Davis, who was there with Noemi’s 16-week-old granddaughter, Blaire. Priscilla Wanerus then suggested that by going just a little further up Prospect and then going onto Ranleigh Way, the walkers could enjoy another one of Piedmont’s hidden pathways. This 197-foot path between Ranleigh and the lower portion of Wildwood Avenue across from Wildwood school, was too easy and too enticing to pass up. A walk through Piedmont Park allowed Jane Holland’s K-9 best friend Sasha to have an off-leash run while the rest of the walkers to returned to the Community Hall. The group enjoyed two wonderful weeks of native gardens walks with Hope. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome by registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. BOD tied it 2-2 in the second with a goal in the first 50 seconds, but Nate Fredericks found Dixon for his third goal with 10:44 to go. From there, Von Metzsch made three saves before Fredericks tossed a long ball over the O’Dowd defense toward Spencer Settlemier, who retrieved the ball on a bounce and darted toward the net, unloading for a goal with 7:40 to go. BOD scored with 5:42 and 5:03 remaining to tie the game at 4-4. Piedmont closed the second quarter with Jack Nelson flicking an assist to Dixon with 2:04 left. In the closing seconds, PHS scored again with a man-advantage when Dixon found Settlemier for the goal and a 6-4 advantage at halftime. O’Dowd opened the third quarter with two straight goals at 9:27 and 9:06 to tie the game again at 6-6. With 7:10 left, Nelson had a ground ball recovery in the attacking area, weaved by a defender, and landed the go-ahead goal, 7-6. O’Dowd scored with 20.5 seconds left for another tie, 7-7. In the final quarter, Fredericks scored on a low underhand shot with a man-advantage in the first 30 seconds of play. Nelson scored again with 9:53 on the clock, while Dixon assisted Fredericks with a pass from behind the net with 9:14 left in the game as PHS jumped ahead, 10-7. From there, Von Metzsch stonewalled BOD with three critical saves at 7:14, 6:51, and 6:34 left in the game. She also wanted the cities where we live to be fun and not be boring and static. This quote of Jacobs from a speech she made in 2002 sums up exactly how I feel relative to my various thoughts, observations and suggestions made relative to our built environment: “The suggestions I’ve made may not be politically possible. There may be better or different means of accomplishing similar aims. My purpose is to help stir up creative thinking about how to enlist time and change as practical allies, not as enemies that must be regulated out and fended off on the one hand, or mentally surrendered to, on the other. We might as well learn how to make constructive alliances with the workings of time because time [and change] is going to continue happening”. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. New and Old Buildings Together: buildings that vary in age and condition make for economic diversity and aesthetic character. This is evident in both the new high school and the relatively new Havens Elementary School where thoughtful planning and architecture response to older existing buildings provide interest and a rich historic texture to the place. Density: a sufficient number of people is necessary for the vitality, interest and safety of any city, as shown in this wonderful 3-story area of Mexico City’s Zócalo. In the center of Piedmont the raised three story portion of the Albert Farr-designed Piedmont Community Church suggests that a limited number of additional stories for increased density is not aesthetically objectionable.
